holocene.title: Holocene
holocene.subtitle: 0.012 Ma to Present · The Age of Humanity
holocene.body: Earth is in the Holocene epoch, a warm interglacial period that began about twelve thousand years ago as the last great ice sheets retreated from the Northern Hemisphere. Forests, grasslands, and wetlands spread across the continents, creating a stable and productive biosphere. Megafauna like woolly mammoths and giant ground sloths vanish early in this epoch, likely through a combination of hunting pressure and rapid climate shifts. Modern humans flourish in this window of relative climatic stability, developing agriculture, cities, and civilizations. Sea levels rise more than one hundred meters as glaciers melt, reshaping coastlines worldwide. The biodiversity of today, from tropical rainforests teeming with insects to coral reefs filled with fish, is a product of this remarkable period of ecological recovery and climatic calm that has lasted to the present day.

mid_pleistocene.title: Mid Pleistocene
mid_pleistocene.subtitle: ~1 Ma · Ice Ages and Giants
mid_pleistocene.body: Earth is locked in the rhythm of the Pleistocene ice ages, a pattern of glacial advance and retreat that has dominated the planet for nearly two million years. Around one million years ago, the Mid-Pleistocene Transition reshapes these cycles, shifting from forty-thousand-year glacial pulses to longer and more intense one-hundred-thousand-year cycles. Vast ice sheets periodically smother North America, Europe, and Asia, locking up so much water that sea levels drop by more than a hundred meters, creating land bridges between continents. Megafauna thrive in this cold world: woolly mammoths, cave lions, giant short-faced bears, and the massive Megaloceros elk roam the tundra and steppes. Early members of our genus Homo are spreading out of Africa, crafting stone tools and adapting to wildly different environments across the Old World. Life is tough, cold, and spectacular.

early_quaternary.title: Early Quaternary
early_quaternary.subtitle: ~2 Ma · Dawn of the Ice Age
early_quaternary.body: Earth enters the Quaternary period around two and a half million years ago, and the world is transforming dramatically. Global temperatures have been cooling for millions of years, and now permanent ice caps lock onto the poles. Ice sheets begin their first major advances across the Northern Hemisphere, and the cyclical pattern of glacials and interglacials that will define the next two million years takes hold. In Africa, the grasslands are expanding, and a remarkable group of upright-walking hominins is diversifying. Homo habilis and later Homo erectus emerge, crafting simple stone tools and beginning to spread beyond their African homeland. Megafauna are widespread and varied, with mastodons, early horses, and giant hyenas competing across the continents. The oceans are cool, and the reshaping of ocean circulation patterns drives further climate change, creating the volatile, ice-age world that will ultimately forge modern humanity.

late_neogene.title: Late Neogene
late_neogene.subtitle: ~5 Ma · The Cooling World
late_neogene.body: Earth is a world in the grip of long-term cooling, and the landscapes reflect this shift. Around five million years ago, the Mediterranean Sea repeatedly dries out during the Messinian Salinity Crisis, leaving a vast desert basin before being catastrophically reflooded by the Atlantic. The closure of the Central American Seaway is redirecting ocean circulation and intensifying Northern Hemisphere cooling. Grasslands expand across Africa, Asia, and the Americas, driving the evolution of fast, grazing mammals with high-crowned teeth suited to tough grass. In Africa, the diverging ape lineage is producing australopithecines, our most recognizable bipedal ancestors. Horses, rhinos, elephants, and camels diversify across multiple continents. Polar ice is building, and the world is heading toward the deep freeze of the Quaternary. The continents are nearly in their modern positions, and the ecosystems, though unfamiliar in species, begin to feel recognizable.

mid_neogene.title: Mid Neogene
mid_neogene.subtitle: ~15 Ma · The Miocene Climatic Optimum
mid_neogene.body: Earth is experiencing one of the warmest periods of the last thirty million years. During the Miocene Climatic Optimum, global temperatures peak and forests extend closer to the poles than at any time since the Eocene. The grasslands that will eventually dominate the continents are just beginning to spread, and grazing mammals are starting their long evolutionary journey of specialization. Great ape diversity is at its peak in Africa and Eurasia, with dozens of species occupying forest and woodland niches. Kelp forests appear for the first time in the cooling oceans, and marine mammals like seals, sea lions, and early baleen whales are diversifying rapidly. The Tethys Sea has largely closed, and the collision of Africa with Europe is building the Alps and Mediterranean mountain chains. Antarctica is fully glaciated, driving cold deep-water circulation patterns that will define the modern ocean.

early_neogene.title: Early Neogene
early_neogene.subtitle: ~20 Ma · A World Without Grass
early_neogene.body: Earth at twenty million years ago is a warmer, greener world than today, with forests stretching deep into the mid-latitudes and very little ice beyond the growing Antarctic sheet. The Miocene has just begun, and the mammals that dominate the continents are strange to modern eyes. Early horses are small and three-toed, browsing leaves in warm forests. Mastodons are spreading out of Africa, and the first members of the deer and bovid families are appearing. Apes are abundant and diverse in African and Eurasian forests, occupying ecological roles that monkeys and other primates will later claim. In the seas, sharks, bony fish, and marine mammals are all flourishing. The continents are drifting into configurations close to today, and the collision of India with Asia has already raised the Himalayan peaks. Global circulation is shifting as oceanic gateways open and close, slowly setting the stage for the ice ages to come.

late_paleogene.title: Late Paleogene
late_paleogene.subtitle: ~35 Ma · The Great Cooling
late_paleogene.body: Earth is undergoing a dramatic climatic transition. Around thirty-four million years ago, at the Eocene-Oligocene boundary, the planet experiences one of its most significant cooling events since the end of the Cretaceous. Antarctica becomes fully isolated by the opening of the Drake Passage and the Tasmanian Gateway, allowing the Antarctic Circumpolar Current to form and lock the southern continent in ice. Global temperatures plummet, sea levels fall, and many tropical species go extinct. Forests retreat toward the equator, and the first grasslands begin to appear. The warm, dense jungles of the Eocene give way to more seasonal, open woodlands. Mammals are diversifying rapidly in this new cooler world, with the forerunners of modern horses, rhinos, and early ruminants spreading across the continents. The world is recognizably modern in its physical geography but still exotic in its inhabitants.

mid_paleogene.title: Mid Paleogene
mid_paleogene.subtitle: ~50 Ma · The Warm Eocene World
mid_paleogene.body: Earth at fifty million years ago is one of the warmest it has been in the last sixty-six million years. Dense tropical forests reach as far as the Arctic Circle, where alligators and giant tortoises have been found as fossils. There are no polar ice caps, and sea levels are high. The mammals that survived the end-Cretaceous extinction have been diversifying explosively, and many of the major modern orders are now recognizable. Early whales, the Archaeoceti, are in the process of returning to the sea from land-dwelling ancestors. Horses the size of dogs, early primates, and giant flightless birds called Gastornis are roaming the forests. In the oceans, modern bony fish families are well established, and seagrass meadows provide rich coastal habitat. The world is lush, warm, and teeming with a new generation of mammals rapidly filling every ecological niche left vacant by the dinosaurs.

early_paleogene.title: Early Paleogene
early_paleogene.subtitle: ~60 Ma · Mammals Inherit the Earth
early_paleogene.body: Earth is in the earliest stages of its post-dinosaur recovery. Just six million years have passed since the catastrophic end-Cretaceous extinction, and life is rebounding with remarkable speed. Mammals, once small nocturnal insectivores living in the shadow of the dinosaurs, are now free to diversify into every available niche. Small, generalist species are quickly giving rise to larger and more specialized forms. The first Condylarths, the ancestors of many modern hoofed mammals, are spreading across the continents. The world is warm and forested, with dense vegetation covering much of the land. Birds, having survived the extinction event as the descendants of small feathered dinosaurs, are also diversifying rapidly, including large flightless predatory forms. In the oceans, sharks and bony fish dominate, and the early ancestors of modern whales are still fully terrestrial mammals living near water. The age of mammals has truly begun.

late_cretaceous.title: Late Cretaceous
late_cretaceous.subtitle: ~75 Ma · The Dinosaur Dynasties
late_cretaceous.body: Earth is a world ruled by dinosaurs at their most spectacular and diverse. The continents are separated by warm, shallow inland seas, and global temperatures are significantly warmer than today with no polar ice. In North America, the Western Interior Seaway divides the continent, and along its shores, ceratopsians like Triceratops, hadrosaurs, and tyrannosaurs compete in lush floodplain ecosystems. In Asia, different lineages of tyrannosaurs and feathered dinosaurs flourish. Flowering plants, the angiosperms, have exploded in diversity and are rapidly transforming terrestrial ecosystems, providing new food sources for insects, birds, and small mammals. The oceans are filled with mosasaurs, plesiosaurs, and enormous ammonites. Pterosaurs like Quetzalcoatlus, with wingspans rivaling small aircraft, soar above the treetops. This world of giants and diversity is about to meet its violent end, but for now it represents the magnificent peak of the Mesozoic.

mid_cretaceous.title: Mid Cretaceous
mid_cretaceous.subtitle: ~100 Ma · The Greenhouse Peak
mid_cretaceous.body: Earth at one hundred million years ago is in one of the hottest periods of the entire Mesozoic. Global temperatures peak in the mid-Cretaceous Thermal Maximum, with polar regions free of ice and tropical sea surface temperatures reaching extreme highs. High carbon dioxide levels drive a massive greenhouse effect. Shallow seas flood across the continents, and enormous chalk deposits form across Europe and North America from the shells of trillions of microscopic marine organisms. In these warm oceans, giant marine reptiles and fish thrive alongside an abundance of ammonites and belemnites. On land, the dinosaur fauna is highly diverse. Spinosaurs stalk rivers in Africa, while Carcharodontosaurids are the apex predators. The first flowering plants are beginning their dramatic diversification, fundamentally reshaping terrestrial ecosystems. Early mammals are small but growing more diverse, and feathered dinosaurs occupy a remarkable range of ecological niches.

early_cretaceous.title: Early Cretaceous
early_cretaceous.subtitle: ~130 Ma · Feathers and Flowers
early_cretaceous.body: Earth at one hundred and thirty million years ago is a world on the cusp of dramatic biological transformation. The supercontinent Gondwana is continuing to break apart, isolating South America, Africa, India, and Antarctica on their long separate journeys. In China and elsewhere, exquisite fossils from this period reveal an astonishing diversity of feathered dinosaurs, many with elaborate plumage for display or insulation. The first true birds are diversifying alongside their non-avian relatives. Angiosperms, the flowering plants, are just appearing in the fossil record and are beginning the ecological revolution that will eventually make them the dominant plant group on Earth. Long-necked sauropods still roam, though they are becoming less dominant as ornithopod dinosaurs spread. Spinosaurs are at their peak diversity. The seas are rich with ammonites, and ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs patrol the open water, while reef-building rudist bivalves are transforming shallow marine environments.

late_jurassic.title: Late Jurassic
late_jurassic.subtitle: ~150 Ma · The Age of Giants
late_jurassic.body: Earth at one hundred and fifty million years ago is a world of giants. The Late Jurassic is perhaps the most iconic interval of dinosaur history, populated by some of the largest land animals ever to walk the Earth. In North America and Europe, sauropods like Brachiosaurus and Diplodocus stretch their necks into the forest canopy to feed on ferns and conifers. Predators like Allosaurus stalk the landscape in pursuit of prey. The famous Morrison Formation of North America is forming in this period, preserving a rich snapshot of this world. Archaeopteryx, often called the first bird, is gliding through the forests of what is now Germany. Stegosaurs with their iconic plated backs are widespread. The oceans are warm and rich, filled with ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs, and diverse sharks. The continents of Pangaea have been splitting apart for millions of years, and the Atlantic Ocean is widening slowly.

mid_jurassic.title: Mid Jurassic
mid_jurassic.subtitle: ~165 Ma · Dinosaurs Rise to Dominance
mid_jurassic.body: Earth at one hundred and sixty-five million years ago is firmly in the middle of the Jurassic period, and dinosaurs have consolidated their dominance over the terrestrial world. The supercontinent Pangaea has now fully split into Laurasia in the north and Gondwana in the south, and the Tethys and growing Atlantic Oceans separate these landmasses. This continental reorganization is beginning to drive the evolution of distinct regional faunas. Sauropods are everywhere and reaching enormous sizes. Early stegosaurs are appearing, and feathered coelurosaur dinosaurs are diversifying. The forests are dominated by cycads, conifers, ferns, and horsetails, creating dense green landscapes very different from today. In the oceans, ichthyosaurs are at peak diversity, and the first modern coral reef ecosystems are beginning to form. Mammals remain small and mostly nocturnal, but they are quietly evolving the complex teeth and reproductive strategies that will one day make them masters of the Earth.

early_jurassic.title: Early Jurassic
early_jurassic.subtitle: ~195 Ma · Life After the Great Dying
early_jurassic.body: Earth is recovering from the devastating Triassic-Jurassic mass extinction, which wiped out roughly eighty percent of species just a few million years before this time. The world is warming again from pulses of massive volcanic activity, and the recovering ecosystems are being rapidly colonized by new and diversifying groups. Dinosaurs, having survived the extinction, now face far less competition and begin their dramatic radiation into the many forms that will define the Jurassic. Early sauropods grow larger, and the first true stegosaur and ankylosaur ancestors are appearing. In the oceans, ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs are diversifying into the niches vacated by extinct marine reptiles. The supercontinent Pangaea is actively rifting, and the earliest Atlantic Ocean is opening as a narrow seaway between what will become North America and Africa. Conifer forests are spreading across the warming continents, and insects buzz through increasingly lush vegetation.

late_triassic.title: Late Triassic
late_triassic.subtitle: ~215 Ma · The Rise of the Dinosaurs
late_triassic.body: Earth at two hundred and fifteen million years ago is in a world where dinosaurs are rising but not yet dominant. Pangaea remains largely intact, and the supercontinent creates extreme continental climates with monsoonal rainfall patterns. The Triassic is a time of recovery and radiation following the catastrophic Permian-Triassic extinction, and the ecological niches are contested by multiple groups. Aetosaurs, phytosaurs, and rauisuchians, large crocodile-like archosaurs, still compete with early dinosaurs for dominance on land. The first true mammals appear in this period, tiny shrew-like creatures living alongside their reptilian relatives. Early pterosaurs take to the air, becoming the first vertebrates capable of powered flight. Diverse marine reptiles patrol the oceans, including ichthyosaurs and nothosaurs. This period will end abruptly with another mass extinction triggered by the eruption of the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province, clearing the way for the Age of Dinosaurs.

mid_triassic.title: Mid Triassic
mid_triassic.subtitle: ~235 Ma · Recovery and Radiation
mid_triassic.body: Earth at two hundred and thirty-five million years ago is still in the process of recovering from the most severe mass extinction in its history, the Permian-Triassic event of seventeen million years prior. Life is diversifying rapidly to fill the ecological vacuum, and the pattern of recovery is uneven and fascinating. In the oceans, marine reptiles including the first ichthyosaurs and early placodonts are thriving in warm shallow seas. On land, the archosaurs, the group that includes crocodilians, pterosaurs, and dinosaurs, are diversifying from smaller ancestors. The very first true dinosaurs are just beginning to appear in the fossil record. Rhynchosaurs, large herbivorous reptiles with hooked beaks, are among the most common land animals. Dicynodont therapsids, survivors from the Permian, still populate many landscapes. Pangaea is a single great landmass with enormous deserts in its interior and lush coastal regions. The stage is being set for the age of dinosaurs.

early_triassic.title: Early Triassic
early_triassic.subtitle: ~245 Ma · The Aftermath of Annihilation
early_triassic.body: Earth at two hundred and forty-five million years ago is slowly, painfully pulling itself out of the worst biological catastrophe in its history. Just seven million years have passed since the Permian-Triassic extinction devastated over ninety percent of all species. Recovery is sluggish compared to previous mass extinctions, hampered by repeated pulses of volcanic activity, ocean anoxia, and extreme greenhouse temperatures. The oceans are still largely hostile, with dead zones persisting for millions of years. On land, the therapsid Lystrosaurus dominates in extraordinary abundance, making up the vast majority of large land animals in a world with almost no ecological diversity. Gradually, more complex ecosystems begin to rebuild. Early archosaurs appear and begin to diversify. Microbial mats dominate many marine environments where complex life cannot yet gain a foothold. This is a world on the knife-edge of survival, slowly groping its way back toward complexity.

late_permian.title: Late Permian
late_permian.subtitle: ~260 Ma · Before the Great Dying
late_permian.body: Earth at two hundred and sixty million years ago is home to the most complex terrestrial ecosystems to have yet evolved on land. Pangaea is fully assembled, and vast deserts dominate the continental interior while lush wetlands and forests line the coasts and equatorial zones. The dominant land vertebrates are the therapsids, or mammal-like reptiles, which include ferocious predators like gorgonopsids and large herbivorous dicynodonts. The pareiasaurs, massive barrel-bodied reptiles, are the largest plant eaters of their time. Pelycosaurs like the sail-backed Dimetrodon, though now extinct, were dominant in the earlier Permian. Insects are diverse and some reach giant sizes in oxygen-rich air. Glossopteris forests spread across the southern reaches of Pangaea. In the oceans, complex reef systems built by corals and bryozoans teem with life. This rich and diverse world has just over eight million years before the Siberian Traps eruptions begin one of the greatest catastrophes in the history of life.

mid_permian.title: Mid Permian
mid_permian.subtitle: ~275 Ma · Therapsids Take Over
mid_permian.body: Earth at two hundred and seventy-five million years ago is a world in transition, as one ruling group of vertebrates gives way to another. The great pelycosaurs, including sail-backed Dimetrodon, which dominated the earlier Permian landscape, are giving way to their evolutionary descendants, the therapsids. This group, often called mammal-like reptiles, is becoming the most diverse and ecologically dominant group of large land vertebrates. Among the therapsids, the dicynodonts are the most successful herbivores, while the gorgonopsids are fierce pack predators. The global climate is drying as Pangaea consolidates, with massive interior deserts forming across the supercontinent. Glossopteris trees dominate the Gondwana landmass in the south, forming enormous coal-forming swamp forests. The Tethys Sea, a warm shallow equatorial ocean, supports rich marine communities of corals, brachiopods, and cephalopods. The seeds of the Permian world are sown, though extinction looms ahead.

early_permian.title: Early Permian
early_permian.subtitle: ~290 Ma · Pangaea Takes Shape
early_permian.body: Earth at two hundred and ninety million years ago is in the process of final continental assembly. The great supercontinent Pangaea is nearly complete as Euramerica collides with Gondwana, building the Variscan and Appalachian mountain ranges in the process. These new mountains transform atmospheric circulation and contribute to a significant drying of the continental interior. The coal swamp forests of the Carboniferous are retreating as the climate shifts, and the ecosystems are adapting rapidly. On land, the amniotes, the group of vertebrates whose eggs can be laid on dry land, are diversifying into the ecological space left as the amphibians retreat. Early reptiles and the primitive pelycosaurs, including the iconic sail-backed Dimetrodon, are the dominant large predators. Ferns, seed ferns, and early conifers are diversifying. Glaciation in the Southern Hemisphere is extensive but beginning to wane. The oceans remain rich with brachiopods, corals, and cephalopods, and marine diversity is high.

late_carboniferous.title: Late Carboniferous
late_carboniferous.subtitle: ~305 Ma · The Coal Age
late_carboniferous.body: Earth at three hundred and five million years ago is draped in the vast tropical coal swamp forests that will become the coal deposits powering future industrialization. Towering lycopsid trees thirty meters tall, giant horsetails, and enormous seed ferns create dense, humid forests across the equatorial regions of the assembling Pangaea supercontinent. The high oxygen content of the atmosphere, perhaps as high as thirty-five percent, allows insects and other arthropods to reach extraordinary sizes. Meganeura, a dragonfly-like creature with a wingspan of over sixty centimeters, patrols the forest canopy. Giant millipedes over two meters long crawl the forest floors. Reptiles are diversifying, and early amniotes are beginning to exploit environments away from water. Amphibians remain dominant in the wetlands. Glaciation grips the southern polar regions while the equatorial belt is hot and wet. This complex, high-oxygen world is full of spectacular life, though it is vulnerable to ecological collapse.

mid_carboniferous.title: Mid Carboniferous
mid_carboniferous.subtitle: ~320 Ma · Giants of the Coal Forests
mid_carboniferous.body: Earth at three hundred and twenty million years ago is blanketed in its most famous ancient biome, the Carboniferous coal forests. Across what is now Europe, North America, and parts of Asia, vast lowland swamps support towering lycopod trees that can reach forty meters in height. These forests are productive and dense, with thick mats of vegetation building up organic matter that will one day become some of the world's most important coal deposits. The amphibian fauna has diversified into many ecological roles, with large predatory forms ruling the waterways. The first reptiles have recently evolved, and amniote eggs are freeing these new vertebrates from dependence on standing water to reproduce. Flying insects are extraordinarily diverse, filling the air above the forest canopy. Sharks and bony fish dominate the shallow seas that separate the coalescing landmasses. The great glaciation of Gondwana continues in the south, and the interplay of glacial cycles and tropical forests creates a complex, dynamic world.

early_carboniferous.title: Early Carboniferous
early_carboniferous.subtitle: ~345 Ma · A World Turned Green
early_carboniferous.body: Earth at three hundred and forty-five million years ago is experiencing the expansion of forests across the continental interiors for the first time in its history. Following the Late Devonian extinction, marine diversity is still recovering, but on land a remarkable transformation is occurring. Vast forests of early trees, including the earliest lycopods, ferns, and seed-bearing plants, are spreading across low-lying continents. The colonization of the land by complex plant ecosystems is drawing down enormous quantities of carbon dioxide, cooling the planet and beginning the long atmospheric oxygen rise that will peak in the late Carboniferous. Amphibians are the dominant large land vertebrates, exploiting the rich insect and invertebrate communities of the new forests. The seas are recovering slowly, with sharks diversifying rapidly in warm coastal waters and early coral reef ecosystems rebuilding. The shallow Carboniferous seas of Europe and North America are warm and productive, accumulating the limestone deposits that characterize this period.

late_devonian.title: Late Devonian
late_devonian.subtitle: ~370 Ma · When Fish Grew Legs
late_devonian.body: Earth at three hundred and seventy million years ago is witnessing one of the most transformative transitions in the history of vertebrate life. Lobe-finned fish in shallow coastal swamps and river systems are evolving stronger fins supported by bones, gradually adapted for supporting their bodies out of water. Tiktaalik and its relatives are among the transitional forms bridging the gap between fish and four-limbed tetrapods. The first true amphibians, like Ichthyostega, are hauling themselves onto land. The land is increasingly vegetated, with the first forests of tall tree-ferns and early seed plants spreading across the margins of Gondwana and Laurussia. Fish diversity is extraordinary, dominated by the armored placoderms in the oceans and freshwater environments. The seas are rich with corals, brachiopods, and the devastating predator Dunkleosteus, whose scissor-like bony jaws could crush almost anything. The world is on the verge of major ecological change, both on land and in the sea.

mid_devonian.title: Mid Devonian
mid_devonian.subtitle: ~390 Ma · The Age of Fishes
mid_devonian.body: Earth at three hundred and ninety million years ago is in the midst of the Age of Fishes, a time when the oceans, rivers, and lakes are dominated by an astonishing diversity of aquatic vertebrates. The placoderms, heavily armored jawed fish, are the apex predators in most aquatic environments, and none is more feared than the massive Dunkleosteus, whose bony jaws exert crushing force on prey. Sharks are diversifying in the warm seas, and the first ray-finned and lobe-finned fish are evolving in freshwater and coastal environments. On land, the first forests are beginning to spread. The Devonian is the epoch of trees, with the earliest woody plants like Archaeopteris establishing the first true forested landscapes. Insects and other arthropods are colonizing the land in increasing numbers. Trilobites remain common in the seas, and great reefs built by stromatoporoids and tabulate corals fringe the shallow continental shelves of the supercontinent Gondwana and the smaller northern landmasses.

early_devonian.title: Early Devonian
early_devonian.subtitle: ~410 Ma · Plants Conquer the Land
early_devonian.body: Earth at four hundred and ten million years ago is undergoing a biological revolution on land. For billions of years, the continents were largely barren rock and dust, with only thin microbial crusts and simple organisms clinging to damp coastal areas. Now, in the Early Devonian, the first true vascular plants with roots and water-conducting tissues are spreading inland from coastal marshes and riverbanks. These early plants, including Cooksonia and Aglaophyton, are small and leafless, but they are transforming the soil and atmosphere. The decay of plant matter is creating complex soil ecosystems for the first time. Millipedes and other arthropods follow the plants inland. In the seas, the rich Silurian marine world continues, with jawed fish diversifying rapidly. Placoderms are emerging as the dominant fish group. Coral reefs are spreading. On land, the Devonian plant revolution is a slow but irresistible force that will fundamentally change the planet forever.

late_silurian.title: Late Silurian
late_silurian.subtitle: ~420 Ma · Ancient Seas and Shore Life
late_silurian.body: Earth at four hundred and twenty million years ago is a world where life is beginning its tentative conquest of the land in earnest. The oceans are warm and rich, teeming with trilobites, brachiopods, enormous sea scorpions called eurypterids, and diverse jawless and early jawed fish. Coral reefs fringe the tropical continental shelves, building great carbonate banks. In coastal and freshwater environments, the first vascular plants are taking root, their simple stems and root-like structures anchoring in mud and sand. Small millipede-like arthropods are among the first animals to accompany the plants onto dry land. The Silurian continents are largely concentrated in the Southern Hemisphere, with the great southern supercontinent Gondwana and a cluster of smaller northern landmasses. Sea levels are relatively high after the end-Ordovician glaciation, and shallow seas cover much of the continental interiors. The world is preparing for the dramatic colonization of land that will define the coming Devonian period.

mid_silurian.title: Mid Silurian
mid_silurian.subtitle: ~430 Ma · Reefs and Sea Scorpions
mid_silurian.body: Earth at four hundred and thirty million years ago is recovering from the end-Ordovician mass extinction and hosting a diverse, flourishing marine world. Warm, shallow tropical seas spread across much of the low-latitude continental shelves, and the first true coral reefs are building complex three-dimensional habitats. These ancient reefs are constructed by tabulate and rugose corals, very different from their modern relatives but ecologically just as important. Eurypterids, the great sea scorpions, are among the most fearsome predators in freshwater and brackish environments, with some species reaching over two meters in length. Jawless fish are common in coastal waters, and the first jawed fish, including early sharks, are just beginning to appear. Graptolites, colonial floating organisms, still drift in vast swarms through the open ocean. On land, the first patchwork communities of tiny plants and primitive arthropods are just beginning to establish a toehold in damp coastal environments.

early_silurian.title: Early Silurian
early_silurian.subtitle: ~440 Ma · Recovery After Extinction
early_silurian.body: Earth at four hundred and forty million years ago is in the early stages of recovery following the devastating end-Ordovician mass extinction that wiped out roughly eighty-five percent of marine species just a few million years earlier. As glaciers retreat and sea levels rise again, the shallow continental shelf environments are being recolonized by survivors. Brachiopods, corals, and trilobites are rebuilding their communities, and ecological complexity is returning. The graptolites, bizarre colonial organisms that floated in vast ocean-wide swarms and left beautiful fossils, are still diverse and using the open ocean. Jawless fish continue to diversify in coastal waters. The world is almost entirely ocean, with scattered continental landmasses concentrated in the south. The atmosphere is low in oxygen compared to today, but land is beginning to receive its first visitors. Simple non-vascular plants and pioneering arthropods are beginning the slow colonization of the continental margins.

late_ordovician.title: Late Ordovician
late_ordovician.subtitle: ~450 Ma · Ocean World
late_ordovician.body: Earth at four hundred and fifty million years ago is a world almost entirely dominated by the ocean. The continents, mostly dry barren rock with only the faintest hints of primitive land plants on coastal margins, are scattered and largely concentrated around the equator and Southern Hemisphere. The oceans are warm, rich, and extraordinarily diverse, hosting the product of the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event. Trilobites are everywhere and have diversified into hundreds of ecological roles. Brachiopods form great shell beds on the sea floor. Nautiloid cephalopods, some several meters long, are the apex predators. Graptolites drift in immense colonies through the open ocean. Bizarre echinoderms like crinoids and blastoids filter food from the currents. Jawless fish are becoming more common. This incredibly rich marine world is approaching its end, however. Glaciers are beginning to form on the southern polar continent of Gondwana, and the sea level fluctuations and cooling they trigger will bring catastrophe to the shallow-water communities.

mid_ordovician.title: Mid Ordovician
mid_ordovician.subtitle: ~465 Ma · The Great Biodiversification
mid_ordovician.body: Earth at four hundred and sixty-five million years ago is experiencing one of the greatest explosions of marine biodiversity in its history, the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event. The variety of marine life has already multiplied several times over since the Cambrian, and the oceans are filling with an astonishing array of new forms. Complex ecological relationships are developing between predators and prey, filter feeders and substrate dwellers, that will define marine ecosystems for hundreds of millions of years. Trilobites, brachiopods, molluscs, echinoderms, and graptolites are all diversifying rapidly. The first coral reefs are appearing, built by tabulate and rugose corals. Large nautiloid cephalopods are the dominant apex predators. Jawless fish are becoming more diverse. On the barren land surfaces, the very first evidence of microbial soil crusts and spore-bearing land plants is beginning to appear in isolated, damp coastal zones. The world is entirely ocean-dominated, but the first tentative steps toward land life are being taken.

early_ordovician.title: Early Ordovician
early_ordovician.subtitle: ~480 Ma · Ancient Seas of Life
early_ordovician.body: Earth at four hundred and eighty million years ago is a world in the aftermath of the Cambrian explosion, still building on the astonishing diversity of body plans that first appeared in that earlier interval. The Early Ordovician oceans are rich and diverse, and the biodiversification event that will define the middle of this period is beginning to accelerate. Trilobites are enormously successful and varied. Nautiloid cephalopods are growing larger and more diverse, becoming important predators. Brachiopods, bryozoans, and echinoderms are spreading across the seafloor. The strange Cambrian organisms like the anomalocaridids have given way to these newer groups. In shallow tropical waters, the first carbonate-secreting communities are laying the groundwork for reef-like structures. Glaciation at the south pole is minimal, and sea levels are high. The land surface remains bare and rocky, though the earliest land-dwelling organisms, simple microbial crusts and possibly the first bryophyte-like plants, may be present on damp shorelines.

late_cambrian.title: Late Cambrian
late_cambrian.subtitle: ~495 Ma · Trilobite Seas
late_cambrian.body: Earth at four hundred and ninety-five million years ago is dominated by warm, shallow seas teeming with the products of the Cambrian evolutionary explosion. Trilobites have become extraordinarily diverse and are the most characteristic animals of the late Cambrian seas. These armored arthropods have colonized every available marine environment, from shallow reef margins to the deep sea floor, and have diversified into hundreds of species with a remarkable variety of eye structures, body forms, and lifestyles. Echinoderms, molluscs, brachiopods, and worm-like animals share the seafloor. The great predatory anomalocaridids of the earlier Cambrian are still present. The first primitive jawless fish, the conodonts and early vertebrates, are swimming in these seas. Multiple extinction events pulse through the late Cambrian, referred to as the Dresbachian and Franconian extinctions, periodically resetting and reshuffling the trilobite fauna. The continents are still scattered, with the great Gondwana supercontinent centered near the South Pole and smaller landmasses drifting across the tropical seas.

mid_cambrian.title: Mid Cambrian
mid_cambrian.subtitle: ~510 Ma · The Burgess Shale World
mid_cambrian.body: Earth at five hundred and ten million years ago is the world made famous by the Burgess Shale of British Columbia. This extraordinary fossil site, preserved when an avalanche of fine mud buried a marine community, gives us a stunning window into a mid-Cambrian ocean ecosystem. The creatures preserved there are unlike anything alive today: Opabinia with its five eyes and grasping frontal appendage, Hallucigenia with legs along its back, Wiwaxia covered in scales and spines. Alongside these bizarre forms swim early arthropods, primitive echinoderms, sponges, and early chordates like Pikaia. Anomalocaris is the apex predator, sweeping prey into its circular mouth. Trilobites are highly diverse and abundant. All the major animal body plans that exist today are already present in some form, encoded in the creatures of this strange, ancient sea. The continents are low, warm, and largely flooded, and the atmosphere contains far less oxygen than today.

early_cambrian.title: Early Cambrian
early_cambrian.subtitle: ~530 Ma · The Dawn of Complex Life
early_cambrian.body: Earth at five hundred and thirty million years ago is at the threshold of a biological revolution. The Cambrian Explosion is in full swing, and the oceans are filling with creatures bearing shells, eyes, claws, and complex body plans for the first time in Earth history. Before this moment, life had been mostly soft-bodied and simple for nearly three billion years. Now, within just tens of millions of years, virtually all the major animal phyla appear in the fossil record. The Chengjiang Biota of China, preserved with extraordinary detail, captures this early Cambrian world: small shrimp-like arthropods, early molluscs, primitive echinoderms, and the first chordates. Predation is a major evolutionary force for the first time, driving an evolutionary arms race between predator and prey that produces the armor, eyes, and escape behaviors we see in modern animals. The world is warm, the oceans shallow, and life is writing entirely new chapters in its ancient story.

cambrian_explosion.title: The Cambrian Explosion
cambrian_explosion.subtitle: 538 Ma · When Animals Invented Themselves
cambrian_explosion.body: Five hundred and thirty-eight million years ago, the history of life on Earth changes forever. In a geological instant spanning perhaps twenty million years, nearly all the major animal body plans that will ever exist appear in the fossil record for the very first time. This is the Cambrian Explosion, one of the most breathtaking events in the four-billion-year story of life. Before this moment, Earth's oceans were populated by soft-bodied, mostly simple organisms like the Ediacaran fauna. Then, suddenly, animals with eyes, jaws, legs, shells, and spines burst onto the scene. Trilobites, anomalocaridids, early molluscs, primitive echinoderms, and our own distant chordate ancestors all appear in this extraordinary window. The evolutionary mechanisms behind the explosion include rising oxygen levels, new ecological opportunities, the evolution of predator-prey dynamics, and the unlocking of key developmental genes. The world will never again see such a rapid genesis of biological form.

great_ordovician_biodiversification.title: Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event
great_ordovician_biodiversification.subtitle: 470 Ma · Life's Greatest Marine Expansion
great_ordovician_biodiversification.body: Four hundred and seventy million years ago, the oceans of Earth are undergoing an explosion of diversity that rivals the Cambrian Explosion in its scale and impact. The Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event sees the number of marine genera increase by a staggering factor of three or four over the course of roughly thirty million years. This is not the origin of new body plans as in the Cambrian, but rather an extraordinary diversification within established groups. Trilobites, brachiopods, cephalopods, echinoderms, and bryozoans are evolving thousands of new species to fill every available ecological niche in the shallow, warm, tropical seas that cover much of the world. The first true coral reefs appear. Complex predator and prey relationships develop, driving evolutionary innovation. Sea floor communities shift from simple two-dimensional mats to complex, stratified three-dimensional habitats. This remarkable expansion establishes the ecological template for marine life that will persist, through extinctions and recoveries, for the next two hundred and fifty million years.

end_ordovician_extinction.title: End-Ordovician Mass Extinction
end_ordovician_extinction.subtitle: 443 Ma · Ice, Anoxia, and Annihilation
end_ordovician_extinction.body: Four hundred and forty-three million years ago, Earth is struck by the second-largest mass extinction event in its history, erasing roughly eighty-five percent of all marine species in two catastrophic pulses. The trigger is glaciation on a massive scale. The supercontinent Gondwana drifts over the South Pole, and enormous ice sheets lock up vast quantities of ocean water. Sea levels plummet by more than one hundred meters, destroying the shallow tropical shelf habitats where most marine life thrives. Global temperatures crash. Then, as the glaciers melt and retreat, a second blow falls: the returning ocean waters are oxygen-starved and toxic, spreading dead zones across the seafloor. Trilobites, graptolites, brachiopods, and corals are decimated. The rich marine world built during the Ordovician Biodiversification Event is torn apart. Some groups are nearly completely wiped out. It is a catastrophe of almost unimaginable scale, yet life clings on, and the survivors will eventually rebuild a new ocean world in the Silurian.

late_devonian_extinction.title: Late Devonian Mass Extinction
late_devonian_extinction.subtitle: 374 Ma · The Kelwasser Event
late_devonian_extinction.body: Three hundred and seventy-four million years ago, a prolonged crisis spanning perhaps twenty-five million years devastates marine life in a series of extinction pulses known collectively as the Late Devonian Mass Extinction. The most severe of these is the Kellwasser Event, which marks the Frasnian-Famennian boundary and wipes out roughly seventy percent of all species. The ancient reef ecosystems, built over tens of millions of years by stromatoporoids and corals, collapse and never fully recover. The trigger is likely multifactorial: the explosive spread of land plants is drawing down carbon dioxide, cooling the climate and reducing atmospheric oxygen in the oceans. Massive volcanic events add stress. The warm-water marine communities, so rich and diverse during the Devonian peak, are especially vulnerable to the cooling temperatures and recurring ocean anoxia. On land, however, the story is different. Tetrapods, the first four-limbed vertebrates, are just beginning to colonize the margins of freshwater environments, and they weather the crisis and go on to inherit the Earth.

carboniferous_rainforest_collapse.title: Carboniferous Rainforest Collapse
carboniferous_rainforest_collapse.subtitle: 307 Ma · When the Coal Forests Fell
carboniferous_rainforest_collapse.body: Three hundred and seven million years ago, the vast tropical coal forests that have blanketed the equatorial regions of Pangaea for tens of millions of years suddenly fragment and collapse. This event, known as the Carboniferous Rainforest Collapse, is triggered by a sharp phase of climate change as glacial cycles intensify and the climate becomes drier and more seasonal. The continuous, unbroken forest belt that stretched across Europe and North America breaks into isolated island refugia separated by increasingly dry open terrain. The ecological consequences are profound. Many species of giant insects, amphibians, and coal-forest plants go extinct as their habitat disappears. Isolated forest patches act as evolutionary crucibles, rapidly driving speciation among the survivors. Crucially, the collapse benefits the amniotes, those vertebrates whose eggs can survive outside water, and particularly the early reptiles and proto-mammals. In the drier, more open world that follows, these groups rapidly diversify, setting the stage for the great reptile dynasties of the Permian and beyond.

permian_triassic_extinction.title: Permian-Triassic Mass Extinction
permian_triassic_extinction.subtitle: 252 Ma · The Great Dying
permian_triassic_extinction.body: Two hundred and fifty-two million years ago, Earth experiences the most catastrophic mass extinction in the history of complex life. In what geologists call the Great Dying, approximately ninety-six percent of all marine species and seventy percent of terrestrial vertebrate species are wiped out in a geological instant, perhaps as little as sixty thousand years. The primary driver is the eruption of the Siberian Traps, an unimaginably massive volcanic event that floods Siberia with lava and injects catastrophic quantities of carbon dioxide, methane, and toxic gases into the atmosphere. Global temperatures spike by as much as ten degrees. Ocean acidification dissolves the shells of marine organisms. Widespread ocean anoxia creates vast dead zones. On land, acid rain devastates forests, and the ozone layer is severely damaged by volcanic chlorine and fluorine. Nearly every ecosystem on Earth collapses. Coral reefs, trilobites, over ninety percent of brachiopod species, and most therapsids are gone. Recovery will take at least ten million years.

triassic_jurassic_extinction.title: Triassic-Jurassic Mass Extinction
triassic_jurassic_extinction.subtitle: 201 Ma · The Extinction That Made the Dinosaurs
triassic_jurassic_extinction.body: Two hundred and one million years ago, another great extinction reshapes life on Earth. The Triassic-Jurassic mass extinction eliminates roughly eighty percent of species over a relatively short interval, clearing away the competitors that have kept dinosaurs from dominating the terrestrial world throughout the Triassic. The culprit is once again volcanism on a massive scale: the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province erupts as Pangaea begins to rift apart, flooding enormous areas with lava and releasing massive pulses of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Global temperatures surge, ocean chemistry is disrupted, and the acid rain and warming prove lethal for many groups. The great phytosaurs, aetosaurs, and most large rauisuchian archosaurs that competed with dinosaurs are wiped out. So too are many marine reptile groups, and nearly all the remaining large amphibian lineages. The survivors, primarily dinosaurs, pterosaurs, crocodylomorphs, and early mammals, inherit a largely empty world and explode into an extraordinary diversity of forms in the Jurassic that follows.

jurassic_marine_revolution.title: Mesozoic Marine Revolution
jurassic_marine_revolution.subtitle: 155 Ma · An Arms Race Beneath the Waves
jurassic_marine_revolution.body: One hundred and fifty-five million years ago, the oceans are in the grip of a profound ecological transformation known as the Mesozoic Marine Revolution. This is not a sudden event but a drawn-out arms race between predators and their prey that reshapes the entire structure of marine ecosystems over tens of millions of years. New and more powerful predators, including teleost fish with crushing teeth, durophagous sharks, marine reptiles, and shell-breaking crabs and lobsters, are forcing dramatic evolutionary responses in their prey. Bivalves and gastropods evolve thicker, more elaborately ornamented shells. Sea urchins migrate downward to burrow into sediment for protection. Brachiopods, which dominated Paleozoic seafloors, are largely replaced by the more mobile bivalves. The ecology of the seafloor is being fundamentally restructured as new predator-prey relationships develop. This revolution is raising the overall complexity and intensity of marine ecosystems to levels never seen before, creating the richly interactive ocean communities that will persist, with modifications, into the modern world.

kpg_extinction.title: K-Pg Mass Extinction
kpg_extinction.subtitle: 66 Ma · The Day the Dinosaurs Died
kpg_extinction.body: Sixty-six million years ago, a catastrophe of almost incomprehensible scale strikes the Earth. An asteroid or comet roughly ten kilometers across slams into the shallow sea of what is now the Yucatan Peninsula of Mexico at tens of thousands of kilometers per hour. The impact releases energy equivalent to billions of nuclear weapons, triggering massive earthquakes, tsunamis, and wildfires across the globe. But the killing blow comes from the billions of tons of material blasted into the upper atmosphere, which block sunlight for months or years, shutting down photosynthesis and collapsing the food chains that depend on it. Temperatures plummet. The non-avian dinosaurs, which have ruled the Earth for over one hundred and sixty million years, are wiped out entirely, along with pterosaurs, mosasaurs, plesiosaurs, ammonites, and roughly seventy-five percent of all species. The survivors include small birds, the feathered descendants of theropod dinosaurs, small mammals, crocodilians, turtles, lizards, and snakes, and from these humble survivors, the modern world will grow.

petm.title: Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum
petm.subtitle: 56 Ma · Earth Overheats
petm.body: Fifty-six million years ago, Earth undergoes one of the most dramatic and rapid climate warming events in the geological record. The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum, or PETM, sees global average temperatures spike by five to eight degrees Celsius within just a few thousand years, a geological instant. The trigger is the massive release of carbon into the atmosphere and ocean, possibly from volcanism associated with the opening of the North Atlantic, methane from destabilized seafloor deposits, or a combination of both. Ocean water becomes warmer and more acidic, and deep-sea sediments dissolve as the carbonate compensation depth rises. Many deep-sea foraminifera species go extinct. On land, the warming reshapes ecosystems dramatically. Mammals are suddenly smaller on average, a phenomenon known as dwarfism under warming conditions, and they disperse rapidly across previously cooler landmasses. Modern mammal orders like primates, artiodactyls, and perissodactyls make their first appearances. The PETM lasts roughly one hundred and seventy thousand years before Earth slowly recovers, making it a compelling ancient analogue for modern human-caused warming.

eocene_oligocene_transition.title: Eocene-Oligocene Transition
eocene_oligocene_transition.subtitle: 34 Ma · The Big Chill
eocene_oligocene_transition.body: Thirty-four million years ago, Earth crosses a climatic threshold from which it does not return. The Eocene-Oligocene Transition is one of the most significant cooling events of the Cenozoic, sometimes called the Grande Coupure in reference to the dramatic turnover it causes in European mammal faunas. The key trigger is the isolation of Antarctica. As Australia drifts northward and South America separates further, the Drake Passage opens and the Tasmanian Gateway widens, allowing the Antarctic Circumpolar Current to flow freely around the southern continent for the first time. This current thermally isolates Antarctica, and within a geologically brief period, massive ice sheets lock onto the continent. Global sea levels fall as water is locked in ice. Temperatures drop by several degrees worldwide, and the dense tropical forests that covered much of the world during the warm Eocene retreat toward the equator. Many warm-adapted species go extinct. The cooler, drier, more seasonal world of the Oligocene that follows sets the stage for the evolution of grasslands and the diversification of grazing mammals.
